n: This chapter is a beautiful poem on wisdom. It begins with mining: people know where to dig for silver and how to refine gold.
Iron is dug from the earth, and copper is smelted from ore.

f.g: In the KJV usually copper or bronze, not modern brass.

n: Miners push back darkness with their lamps, searching the deepest recesses of the earth for ore.

f.g: Ore buried in the dark depths.

n: Far from where people live, miners cut shafts and dangle on ropes, forgotten by travelers above.

f.g: Better “he cuts a shaft” far from settlements.
Better “they dangle and sway” on ropes.

n: The earth’s surface produces bread, while underneath it is turned upside down as if by fire — a picture of mining beneath fields of grain.

f.w: turned up as it were fire
f.g: Possibly the fires miners used to crack rock.

n: Its rocks contain sapphires and its dust holds gold.

f.g: Probably lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone.

n: Miners walk a hidden path that no bird of prey has spotted, not even the sharp-eyed falcon.

f.g: Probably a falcon or kite, famous for keen eyesight.

n: No proud beast or lion has ever walked it. Human skill reaches where even the wildest creatures cannot.

f.g: Literally “sons of pride” — proud, majestic beasts.

n: Human beings attack hard rock and overturn mountains at their roots.

f.w: overturneth the mountains by the roots

n: They cut channels through rock, and their eyes spot every treasure.

f.g: Digs tunnels or drainage channels in mines.

n: They dam up the trickling springs and bring hidden things into the light. Humans are brilliant at finding treasure.
The key question: but where can wisdom be found? Where does understanding live? All our skill at mining can’t dig it up.
People don’t know its true value, and it isn’t found anywhere in the world of the living.
The deep ocean and the sea both say, “It isn’t here.”

f.g: The primeval deep, the waters beneath the earth.

n: Wisdom can’t be bought with gold or weighed out in silver.

f.w: It cannot be gotten for gold

n: It can’t be valued in Ophir’s gold, precious onyx, or sapphire.

f.g: A precious stone, possibly carnelian or onyx.

n: Neither gold nor glass can compare, and it can’t be traded for fine golden jewelry.

f.g: Probably glass, which was rare and costly in ancient times.

n: Coral and crystal aren’t worth mentioning; wisdom is worth more than rubies.

f.w: the price of wisdom is above rubies

n: The topaz of Cush can’t compare, nor can the purest gold.

f.g: Hebrew Cush — the region south of Egypt (modern Sudan).

n: The refrain returns: where then does wisdom come from? Where does understanding dwell?
It is hidden from every living eye, even from the birds that see so much.
Even Destruction and Death say they have only heard a rumor of it.

f.g: Hebrew Abaddon — the realm of the dead, personified.

n: Only God understands the way to wisdom and knows where it lives.
For he sees to the ends of the earth and everything under heaven.

f.w: looketh to the ends of the earth

n: When God gave the wind its weight and measured out the waters…
…when he made a law for the rain and a path for the thunderstorm…

f.w: a way for the lightning of the thunder

n: …then he saw wisdom, appraised it, established it, and searched it out. Wisdom was with God at the Creation.
The poem’s climax: God tells humanity that reverence for the Lord is wisdom, and turning from evil is understanding. This is exactly how Job is described in 1:1.

f.w: the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom

f.g: Reverent awe and devotion, not terror.
